HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      32
Table of annexes
Annexe 1. Lifestyle: tips for better habits 33
Annexe 2. Fibromyalgia. Information to be shared with the patient 34
Annexe 3. Fibromyalgia. Prescription and implementation of adapted physical activity 36
Annexe 4. Fibromyalgia. Patient education: skills to be developed 38

HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      33
Annexe 1. Lifestyle: tips for better habits
Start with an assessment of lifestyle practices, encourage health-promoting behaviours and provide support to make changes if necessary
Increase physical activity
Encourage the person to be as active as their functional capacity allows, adapting their level of exercise to their own physical fitness. Start with small amounts of physical activity (PA), then gradually and moderately increase the fre-quency, intensity and duration to reach the recommended levels in addition to everyday physical activities. The daily duration of moderate-intensity cardiovascular activities (getting slightly out of breath during exercise) combined with muscle strengthening (e.g. climbing stairs) and stretching several times a week can be divided up into sequences of 10 minutes or less.
Reduce sedentary behaviour
Reduce the amount of time spent sitting or lying down as far as possible. Break up sedentary periods every 90 to 120 minutes with short sequences (4/5 min) of movement (walking, simple muscle relaxing movements, etc.), make a few movements to activate muscles and mobilise joints (rotation of shoulders, pelvis, ankles, wrists, hands, head).
Improve diet: meal quality and environment, dietary balance
− Make sure each meal contains nutrients that promote satiety, particularly wholegrain or semi-wholegrain products. Add fresh produce: fruit and vegetables, pulses: lentils, beans, chickpeas, nuts: walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds and unsalted pistachios, etc.
− Encourage home cooking and meal preparation, eating at regular times, allowing enough time to eat (at least 20 minutes), paying attention to the food being eaten, chewing slowly and savouring each mouthful. At the table, avoid screens, films or television programmes, and listening to the news.
− Promote access to dietary assistance if necessary (social worker).
Favour wholemeal or multigrain bread, wholemeal pasta and rice, wholemeal semolina, alternating consumption of oily and lean fish, rapeseed oil, walnut and olive oil, sufficient consumption of dairy products (excluding sweetened milk desserts), limited to 2 servings per day for young adults and 3 to 4 per day for adults over 70 years of age, seasonal foods and locally produced foods. Recommend a Mediterranean-style diet (rich in fruit, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and oily fish) due to its health benefits. It should be noted that the effect on weight loss is increased if the Mediterranean diet is combined with a reduction in dietary energy intake, an increase in physical activity, and im-plementation for more than six months.
Limit the amount and frequency of alcohol, sugary products and drinks, salty products, cured meats, red meat (pork, beef, veal, mutton, lamb, offal), and ultra-processed products. Avoid snacking between meals.
Get enough sleep, maintain good sleep quality and keep to a regular sleep-wake cycle
In the morning, get your biological clock working properly: get up at regular times, expose yourself to sunlight or light, and engage in regular physical activity, which also increases sleep pressure (accumulation of fatigue during the waking period and the need to sleep at the end of the day).
− In the evening, prepare for sleep: learn to limit screen time, go to bed at regular times, prevent night-time food crav-ings: do not skip dinner, eat foods that make you feel full.
− At night, keep your bedroom quiet, cool and dark to promote sleep.
− Engage in physical activity or movement from the morning.
− If necessary, re-establish a regular sleep-wake cycle during the week.
Promote physical, mental and social well-being
− Social activities in all their forms, regular family contact that is experienced as positive, feeling respected, and hav-ing a positive self-image.
− Fulfilling emotional and sex life.
− Good quality of work life: respect, atmosphere, recognition and appreciation of work done, good working conditions, sense of involvement, absence of psychosocial risks (stress, bullying, stigmatisation)

HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      34
Annexe 2. Fibromyalgia. Information to be shared with the patient
What fibromyalgia is and is not
Fibromyalgia is multifactorial and is a chronic pain syndrome. The pain is usually associated with other symptoms and impairs physical capacities, the performance of everyday activities and quality of life. It is not a degenerative disease. It is not dangerous and does not affect vital organs or life expectancy.
Its frequency and the population concerned
The prevalence of fibromyalgia is approximately 1.5 to 2%. It affects more women than men.
Its causes, its origin
Fibromyalgia is linked to changes in the pain detection and modulation processes in the central nervous system, leading to hypersensitivity to pain.
Its main signs and symptoms
− Diffuse pain persisting for more than 3 months, but often variable and fluctuating over time and in intensity and loca-tion.
− Symptoms often associated with the pain, in particular chronic physical fatigue, excessive fatigability on exertion, cog-nitive disturbances (attention and concentration difficulties, memory loss, brain fog), sleep disturbances, emotional distress, psychological disorders (anxiety, depression without necessarily implying a psychological cause for the pain), functional bowel disorders, functional limitations that interfere with activities of daily living, as well as professional, fam-ily and social activities.
− Hypersensitivity of muscles, joints and tendons to touch or pressure, either localised or widespread, that may be asso-ciated with more general hypersensitivity to cold, heat, light, or noise.
Its diagnosis
The diagnosis is clinical, based on the disease history, a physical examination and an in-depth interview with the patient. A process is implemented to investigate for other diseases or conditions with similar symptoms. The existence of fibromyalgia does not exclude the concomitant presence of other diseases.
A small number of laboratory tests are prescribed to screen for diseases, particularly inflammatory or endocrine diseases, which can be treated. Other tests may be required to eliminate other diagnoses.
Its impact on quality of life
Symptoms can interfere with activities of daily living, their planning and their performance, as well as work and inter-personal relationships. The difficulties experienced may vary from person to person and change over time.
The objectives of treatment
In fibromyalgia, the treatment strategy primarily focuses on physical activity, including independent learning so that it can be continued and incorporated into the person’s lifestyle, the development of personalised strategies for self-managing pain and coping with the condition; support to remain in work; support for all forms of vulnerability, treatment and support for other health problems (sleep disturbances, obesity).
Medication has modest effects in terms of alleviating pain. A risk of misuse may exist.
If mood disorders (anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation) are identified, they need to be assessed in order to offer appropriate treatment. These disorders can make it difficult for patients to engage in their treatment and cope with their condition.
A personalised care plan and the essential engagement of the patient
The care plan is developed jointly with the patient based on a shared decision-making approach: information-sharing, supported by a written document [Fibromyalgia.Understanding the disease to better live with its symptoms.]
“Fibromyalgie :
Comprendre la maladie pour mieux vivre avec ses symptômes"
, explanations about the condition and treatment options,
consideration of the patient's expectations and preferences, regular assessment of the effects of treatment, and reformulation of the care plan if necessary.
To start with: offer support in coping with the condition and finding personalised pain management strategies, continuing daily physical activity, choosing an enjoyable physical activity to practise with others (family, friends, clubs, etc.), reducing sedentary behaviour; maintaining good sleep quality; adjusting dietary balance and variety if necessary; and maintaining a regular meal schedule. Encourage continued employment and usual activities as far as possible.

HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      35
The joint assessment by the physician and the patient identifies clinical improvements and those perceived by the patient, as well as difficulties. It makes it possible to propose complementary treatments or approaches.
In the event of difficulties engaging in physical activities independently, supervised adapted physical activity is proposed, to then be continued independently. To help patients become more independent in the management of their condition, patient education sessions are proposed. A specialised and structured psychotherapeutic approach may be proposed in the event of difficulties coping with the condition.
Working with fibromyalgia is possible
Keeping a person with a diagnosis of fibromyalgia in work should be promoted early on and, if applicable, adaptations should be sought with occupational health and prevention service physicians.
Medication has a modest effect
Only certain antidepressants or anticonvulsants are prescribed as background therapy for their analgesic action, even in the absence of a diagnosis of depression or epilepsy. The usual analgesics may be prescribed for incident pain but never as long-term treatment. Opioids should be used with caution and only occasionally for acute incident pain, and should be used only exceptionally as long-term therapy following advice.
Medicinal products are started at low doses to improve their tolerability and reduce the occurrence of adverse effects. Their continuation or discontinuation is assessed in terms of the tolerability and efficacy as perceived by the patient. Misuse is possible and should be identified, along with the associated risks requiring support.
Nutrition
A balanced and varied diet covers the real needs of the individual. Diets with specific restrictions (e.g. gluten-free, lactose-free, low-calorie, low in FODMAP),
46
 the use of nutritional supplements (vitamins, minerals, herbal, etc.), probiot-ics and prebiotics have no demonstrated benefit in fibromyalgia in the absence of proven deficiencies or diagnosed gas-tro-intestinal disorders. There are no arguments for or against a Mediterranean, vegetarian or vegan diet.
Other interventions without adverse effects or health risks may be discussed in the context of the care plan
Hydrotherapy combined with physical exercise has moderate analgesic and/or functional benefits, to be consolidated by independent physical activity.
Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) can be useful to temporarily alleviate flare-ups of localised or locore-gional pain following multidisciplinary advice and in specific prescribing conditions, with patient training, regular monitoring of the effects and discontinuation in the event of inefficacy.
Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) and Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) have a general effect on chronic pain and quality of life. These techniques may be offered in a healthcare facility, following the advice of a chronic pain clinic and depending on their availability.
Relaxation therapy, hypnosis and meditation may have positive effects (state of relaxation, calmness and well-being), provided that they are delivered in accordance with certain conditions, in particular appropriate training of the practitioner, self-learning by the patient.
User associations: experience-sharing, support
User associations share information about fibromyalgia and experiences of living and coping with the condition, provide support to patients, highlight the criteria for vigilance to prevent certain abusive practices, and participate in the design of patient education sessions, co-facilitating them with a healthcare professional following prior training.
46 FODMAP (Fermentescible Oligosaccharides, Disacchararides Monosaccharides And Polyols): naturally poorly digested sugars that ferment when they come into contact with bacteria in the bowel and, when eaten in excess or by sensitive individuals, cause intestinal bloating, leading to pain and gas.

HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      36
Annexe 3. Fibromyalgia. Prescription and implementation of adapted physical activity
 Any prescription for adapted physical activity must be preceded by an assessment
47
Box 1. Content of the medical consultation prior to prescription of adapted physical activity (APA) (HAS.
La prescription d’activité physique adaptée. [Prescribing adapted physical activity] July 2022)
− Full physical examination: cardiovascular, respiratory, cutaneous and locomotor.
− Assessment of the various components of the patient’s physical condition, which may be performed by an APA professional.
− Motivational interview to identify obstacles and levers for physical activity and a more physically active, less sedentary lifestyle.
− Prescription of additional tests and/or a specialised opinion if applicable.
− Scheduling of medical follow-up to assess progress, adjust the prescription, boost patient motivation, and gradually guide patients towards a more physically active, less sedentary life-style, independently and safely.
 In particular, the exercises proposed may include aerobic endurance and muscle-strengthening exercises, along with exercises promoting muscle and joint flexibility and balance
Box 2. Types of physical exercises and implementation methods in fibromyalgia
Progressive, low- to moderate-intensity exercises that are land- or water-based are proposed based on local provision and the patient’s preferences.
In particular, the exercises proposed may include aerobic endurance* and muscle-strengthen-ing** exercises, along with exercises promoting muscle and joint flexibility and balance.
 Aquatic activities have the benefit of being better tolerated due to the relative reduction in weight bearing in water, and of facilitating movement and reducing kinesiophobia.
Sessions take the form of group or individual sessions, delivered 1 to 3 times per week, over a period of 3 months.
 The duration of the sessions, along with their methods, should be adapted based on the patient’s tolerance to exercise, the persistence of pain between sessions and the patient’s availability.
Exercises should be varied and fun to prevent them becoming monotonous and patients giving up during the programme, and to support motivation and effort.
Support for resuming physical activity and continuing it independently with follow-on support is an integral part of the APA programme.
When patients already engage in significant physical activity, the objective is to support them in regulating its intensity to prevent worsening of symptoms.
* Aerobic endurance physical activity: exercise bike, treadmill.
** Muscle-strengthening physical activity: weight machine with guided weights, weights and dumbbells, elastic bands.
47
 Haute Autorité de santé. Guide. Consultation et prescription médicale d’activité physique à des fins de santé chez l’adulte.
[Physical activity consultation and medical prescription on health grounds in adults].
2022. Saint-Denis La Plaine

HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      37
 The prescription is based on “FITT-VP” principles adapted to fibromyalgia
Box 3. FITT-VP characteristics of the physical activity (HAS)
48
− F for frequency: 1 to 3 times per week (for fibromyalgia) over a period of 3 months, potentially renewable following assessment of functional capacities after the programme
− I for intensity, low to start with, then gradually progressing to moderate intensity (patients moderately out of breath and moderate perspiration, conversation possible)
− T for type of physical activity chosen based on the expected physiological effects in terms of improvement: endurance exercises combined with muscle strengthening exercises and, if necessary, flexibility and balance exercises
− T for session time, progressive, intermittent if necessary and without repetition of movements, including a warm-up phase and a recovery phase in addition to the physical activity itself
− V for volume or amount of physical activity: start with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increase the frequency, intensity and duration, paying attention to exercise tolerance, assessment of pain and fatigue before and after each session, and any persistence between sessions
− P for progression, low-intensity physical activity at the start, with slow, controlled progression
 Physical activity is proposed in the form of a programme
Box 4. Characteristics of an adapted physical exercise programme (APA)
‒ Structured and supervised by an adapted physical activity professional
‒ Delivered as a group or individual session
‒ Personalised and therefore appropriate to the patient’s capacities, expectations and preferences
‒ Well tolerated in terms of fatigability, exercise tolerance (working on endurance rather than strength), recovery and possible persistence of pain between sessions, and patient availability
‒ Progressive, with fun, varied exercises to prevent them becoming monotonous and stop patients giving up during the programme, and to support motivation and effort
 The APA professional transmits the programme and a regular report to the prescribing physician
Box 5. Implementation of adapted physical exercise: content of interim assessments
− FITT-VP characteristics of the physical activities: intensity, frequency, progressivity, any flare-ups of pain and/or fatigue, patient perception
− Process, effects on physical condition and functional capacities, ability to perform activities of daily living, including professional activity
− Degree of autonomy in physical activity
− Need to renew the APA prescription or change physical activities if necessary, or continue independently and safely, or refer to a suitable facility
48
 Haute Autorité de santé. Guide. Consultation et prescription médicale d’activité physique à des fins de santé chez l’adulte.
[Physical activity consultation and medical prescription on health grounds in adults].

HAS • Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy • June 2025      38
Annexe 4. Fibromyalgia. Patient education: skills to be developed
Self-care skills
− Learn about fibromyalgia.
− Recognise and know how to assess symptoms, their fluctuations, life situations or events, factors that aggravate,
trigger or maintain pain, and what provides relief based on experience.
− Identify and understand the repercussions of fibromyalgia on activities of daily living and quality of life.
− Recognise own emotions and warning signs (worsening of pain, mood disorder, reduced motivation, etc.).
− Understand the benefits of treatment options, the uncertainties and risks of certain practices, products and methods.
− Recognise own physical capacities and limitations.
− Know how to organise everyday life, simplify activities of daily living, breaking them down into smaller tasks, find a
balance between periods of activity and rest, then work together to develop ways of adapting to the condition and then
moving towards personal coping strategies.
− Regularly participate in adapted physical exercise sessions, know how to continue these independently.
− Implement lifestyle changes: daily physical activity, reducing sedentary behaviour, engage in enjoyable physical
exercise at an appropriate intensity, sleep and life rhythms, diet.
Coping or pyschosocial skills
− Know yourself and accept your limits, rebuild confidence in own abilities.
− Put your feelings and emotions into words, express your fatigue from the daily effort of taking care of yourself.
− Express your needs, expectations, beliefs, perceptions, fears and understanding of your pain.
− Seek help from those around you and involve them in the adjustments made necessary by the condition.
− Identify a feasible plan that takes into account the condition and treatment requirements, set achievable goals and
make choices, proceed in stages.
− Based on your experience and discussions with other patients, develop creative reasoning and critical thinking in the
search for personalised solutions to alleviate symptoms and cope with flare-ups of pain.
− Take decisions and solve problems: adapt your environment, simplify activities of daily living, continue working.
− Develop communication and interpersonal skills, seek support from family, friends and social circles to maintain moti-
vation and facilitate daily life.
− Observe yourself, assess yourself and build your strength.
Educational resources for skills learning
49
Resources
Examples
Patient-centred communication
techniques
Active listening, empathy, encouraging attitude, motivational interviewing to be used
when developing the educational diagnosis, during educational and medical follow-
up, to initiate change in the patient and to support their motivation over time
Teaching techniques
Interactive presentation, case study, round table discussion, brainstorming, critical
analysis of documentary or technological resources, analysis of a situation, experi-
ence or follow-up diary, workshop, physical activities, role playing, documentary
testimony, photolanguage technique®
Tools
Posters, picture books, brochures, technological resources for transmitting, sharing
or exchanging information
49

## p_3689475 : 2025-07-10_fibromyalgia_in_aduts_diagnostic_management_and_treatment_strategy_key_messages_2025_2025-10-03_11-56-44_611

RECOMMENDING BEST PRACTICES
SUMMARY
Fibromyalgia in adults: diagnostic management and treatment strategy
Validated by the HAS Board on 19 June 2025
Key messages
Fibromyalgia is a disease recognised by the World Health Organization, which classes it under the chronic widespread pain grouping (international classification of diseases – ICD 11).
It is linked to changes in pain detection and modulation processes in the central nervous system, manifesting as generalised hypersensitivity to pain. It impairs physical capacities, the performance of activities of daily living and quality of life.
The prevalence of fibromyalgia in the general population is around 1.5 to 2%, with the condition affecting almost three times more women than men.
The diagnosis is a clinical one in the absence of specific biomarkers
‒ Consider fibromyalgia in the event of diffuse pain persisting for more than 3 months, often variable and fluctuating over time and in intensity and location. The pain is combined with other non-specific symptoms, such as fatigue, sleep disturbances, transit disturbances, and cognitive and psychological disorders (anxiety, depression).
‒ Use the self-administered FIRST (Fibromyalgia Rapid Screening Tool) questionnaire in the primary care setting to aid the diagnostic process, but clinical judgement remains the primary factor.
‒ Investigate for other diseases causing chronic pain and concomitant diseases: minimal laboratory tests supplemented on the basis of the physical examination and clinical judgement.
‒ Confirm the diagnosis of fibromyalgia, assess its severity using the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria [revised in 2016].
‒ Repeat the physical examination before attributing any new symptom to fibromyalgia.
Recognising the person’s suffering and delivering the diagnosis are essential
‒ Legitimise their complaints. Deliver in-depth, personalised explanations about the condition, its mechanisms and the treatment options, supported by a written document
1
.
‒ Co-construct the care plan taking into account the patient’s experiences, expectations and preferences: realistic and achievable treatment goals, the most appropriate practitioners and locations for their implementation, and assessment elements defined with the patient.
1
« Fibromyalgie : Comprendre la maladie pour mieux vivre avec ses symptômes"

The treatment strategy is personalised, scaled, coordinated and scalable
‒ Fibromyalgia treatment focuses on getting patients moving again, finding personalised strategies for the self-management of pain and other symptoms, and continuation of everyday activities and work.
‒ The general practitioner coordinates the care plan, along with the professionals involved in its implementation, with, if necessary, an advanced practice nurse or public health nurse
2
 trained in chronic pain, and as part of a coordinated care process.
‒ Referral to other specialist physicians in the community or healthcare facility setting, or to a chronic pain clinic (SDC)
3
 may be necessary for an opinion, advice, multidisciplinary and multi-professional assessment, the choice of, or access to, a treatment, recalcitrant pain, and to a coordination support system (DAC)2 in the event of coordination difficulties.
As a first-line approach
Physical activity and independent, safe exercising
‒ First encourage the maintenance of everyday physical activities, along with regular exercise and a reduction in sedentary behaviour.
‒ If physical activity levels are insufficient and the patient has difficulties exercising autono-mously and safely by themselves: propose an adapted physical activity programme includ-ing independent learning, supervised by an APA professional
4
.
‒ In the event of persistent difficulties or physical deconditioning: refer to a rehabilitation programme based on multidisciplinary, multi-professional assessment.
The development of coping strategies and self-management strategies for the condition
‒ Improve daily functioning and jointly develop coping strategies: simplify daily activities, break them down into smaller tasks, alternate periods of activity with rest periods.
‒ To encourage greater autonomy in managing the condition or in the event of self- management difficulties: collective therapeutic patient education sessions.
‒ In the event of inappropriate behaviours such as catastrophising, an obsessive tendency to work or keep busy all the time, avoidance behaviours: act on cognition (erroneous thoughts, beliefs), emotions and behaviours with specialised and structured psychological interven-tions.
Retention in employment
‒ Seek the support of an occupational health and prevention service physician in the event of a significant impact of the condition on the patient’s work, or of the patient’s work on the condition.
‒ In the event of significant difficulties, and ideally before considering sick leave: seek adaptations in coordination with the occupational health and safety physician.
‒ In the event that the job cannot be adequately adapted: consider training and career guidance measures, recognition as a disabled worker, or an application for disability, some-times temporarily.
2 Assuming a future regulatory extension of their areas of competence to include chronic pain.
3
 SDC: structure spécialisée douleur chronique [specialised chronic pain clinic]; DAC: dispositif d’appui à la coordination [coordination support system].
4 APA : adapted physical activity professionals (in particular adapted physical activity trainers, physiotherapists)

Assessment and treatment of any associated health problems
‒ Situations of overweight and obesity, which are more common in fibromyalgia, linked to inadequate levels of physical activity and sedentary behaviours, must be assessed and treated.
‒ Dietary restrictions (e.g. gluten-free, lactose-free, etc.) and the use of nutritional supplements (vitamins, minerals, herbal, etc.) have no demonstrated benefit in fibromyalgia, in the absence of diagnosed gastrointestinal disorders or proven deficiencies.
‒ A balanced and varied diet covers the real needs of the individual. There are no arguments for or against a Mediterranean, vegetarian or vegan diet.
‒ Sleep disturbances should be investigated and treated.
‒ Psychological disorders (anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation) should be regularly assessed and treated, without necessarily implying a psychological cause for the pain.
‒ Any form of vulnerability should be identified and support provided.
As a second-line approach in addition to first-line interventions
The expected benefit of some medicinal treatments is modest, and opioids should only be used in exceptional circumstances
‒ Start treatments at low doses with a gradual and cautious increase in dosage in order to improve tolerability and reduce the occurrence of adverse effects.
‒ For constant pain and as background therapy: certain antidepressants and anticonvulsants, at low doses.
‒ For incident pain, associated with exertion, for example: the usual analgesics (paracetamol or NSAIDs) on an occasional basis, never as long-term treatment.
‒ For acute incident pain: cautious and occasional use of tramadol (opioid) and as long-term treatment in exceptional cases only, following a specialist opinion in a chronic pain clinic.
‒ Each time a medication prescription is issued or renewed: assess the safety and perceived efficacy, identify any misuse and associated risks.
Other interventions without adverse effects or health risks should be discussed in the context of the care plan
‒ Hydrotherapy if combined with physical exercise and continued independently: in the event of moderate severity of the condition and in a stable phase.
‒ Relaxation, hypnosis, meditation: subject to certain conditions and delivery methods, provided that practitioners are appropriately trained and treatment is discontinued if there is no response.
As a third-line approach following assessment and in addition to first- and second-line interventions
Proposal of neurostimulation techniques subject to certain conditions
‒ In the event of flare-ups of localised or locoregional pain following a multidisciplinary opinion: transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
5
 on a temporary basis.
5 TENS: Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation; rTMS: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (tDCS: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation)

‒ If seeking a general effect on pain and quality of life, following the opinion of a chronic pain clinic: repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS),5 transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS),5 depending on the availability of the technique.
Throughout the care pathway
Support from patient associations
‒ Sharing of reliable information on fibromyalgia, sharing of experiences of living and coping with the condition, support for patients.
‒ Highlighting of the criteria for vigilance to prevent certain abusive practices.
‒ Participation in the design of patient education sessions, co-facilitation with a healthcare professional following prior training.
